title: IIFEs and the module pattern before ESM
hook: Before ECMAScript modules, developers wrapped code in an Immediately Invoked Function Expression (IIFE) to hide private variables and return a public API — the classic module pattern built entirely on closures.

blocks.text: An **IIFE** (Immediately Invoked Function Expression) is a function expression that runs as soon as it is defined: `(function () { ... })()`. Wrapping script code in an IIFE creates a private scope so `var` and inner `function` declarations do not pollute the global object. The **module pattern** returns an object (or function) exposing only chosen methods while keeping state in closure variables — private by construction, not by access modifiers.

entries.plainDefinition: A function expression that is defined and executed immediately, often to create a private scope.
A closure-based pattern returning a public API object while hiding implementation details.
entries.example: const api = (function () { let n = 0; return { inc: () => ++n }; })();

entries.plainDefinition: Native import/export syntax with file-level scope. Preferred over IIFEs in modern apps.
Accidentally attaching names to window/globalThis that collide with other scripts.
entries.example: var utils = {} without a wrapper in two script tags

blocks.text: Legacy codebases, jQuery plugins, and bundled libraries still use IIFEs. Understanding the module pattern explains how JavaScript simulated privacy before classes and `export`. In interviews, you may be asked to implement a counter or config singleton without globals — the module pattern is the canonical answer. Modern code should prefer ES modules, but reading webpack bundles and old Stack Overflow answers requires IIFE fluency.

items.title: Wrap in function expression
items.body: Use (function () { ... })() or (() => { ... })() so the parser treats function as an expression.

items.title: Keep private state inside
items.body: Variables declared inside are not visible outside — only via returned API.

items.title: Return public surface
items.body: Return an object with methods that close over private state.

items.title: Assign or export
items.body: Assign to a single global in legacy scripts; use export in modern modules.

blocks.title: Forgetting parentheses around function expression
blocks.body: function(){}() is invalid — the parser sees a declaration. Use (function(){})() or void function(){}().

blocks.title: Exposing mutable private objects
blocks.body: Returning the internal array directly lets callers mutate private state. Return copies or methods that mediate access.

interviewTakeaways: IIFE = define and invoke immediately to create a private scope without polluting global.
Module pattern returns a public API object; private state lives in closure variables.
ES modules replaced most IIFE use cases but legacy bundles and plugins still use the pattern.
60s: Wrap in (function(){})(), keep secrets inside, return { public methods }. Closures enforce privacy before class private fields.
Follow-up: how does ES module scope differ from an IIFE file wrapper?
commonPitfalls: Using function declaration syntax for IIFE without wrapping parens — SyntaxError.
Returning internal mutable state directly — breaks encapsulation.
Strong answer: 'IIFE for one-shot scope. Module pattern for closure-based API. Prefer ESM today; read IIFEs in legacy code and UMD bundles.'
